body.text: Worked Example 1: Baseline QRE Calculator and ASC Credit Computation

In Scenario A, a company incurs three categories of qualified domestic R&D expenditures during the current taxable year: $500,000 in Box 1 W-2 wages for qualified services (100% eligible = $500,000 on Line 42), $100,000 in tangible non-depreciable supplies consumed in research (100% eligible = $100,000 on Line 43), and $200,000 paid to unrelated U.S. contractors (subject to the 65% limitation under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) = $130,000 on Line 45, with $70,000 [35%] statutorily excluded). While total raw R&D spend is $800,000, total validated QREs on Form 6765 Line 48 equal $730,000 ($500,000 + $100,000 + $130,000).

To demonstrate how this $730,000 QRE figure translates into actual tax credits under Section B (ASC) of Form 6765, assume the taxpayer's validated QREs for the three preceding taxable years were $500,000 (3 years prior), $550,000 (2 years prior), and $600,000 (1 year prior):

items: Total Prior 3-Year QREs (Form 6765, Line 21): $500,000 + $550,000 + $600,000 = $1,650,000 (yielding a 3-year annual average of $1,650,000 ÷ 3 = $550,000).
ASC Base Amount — 50% of 3-Year Average (Form 6765, Line 22): Dividing Line 21 by 6.0 ($1,650,000 ÷ 6.0, which is mathematically identical to 50% × $550,000) equals $275,000.
Excess Current-Year QREs (Form 6765, Line 23): $730,000 - $275,000 = $455,000.

Gross ASC Credit at 14% (Form 6765, Line 24 & Line 25): $455,000 × 14% = $63,700 (requiring the taxpayer to reduce its IRC Section 174A domestic R&E deduction by $63,700 under IRC Section 280C(c)(1) if Item A is checked "No").

Net ASC Credit with IRC § 280C(c)(2) Election (Form 6765, Line 26): If the taxpayer checks "Yes" on Item A of Form 6765 to preserve 100% of its $800,000 Section 174A deduction, the reduced credit is $63,700 × 79% = $50,323.

body.text: Worked Example 2: The "TechFlow Inc." Software Case Study
In Scenario B, a software company ("TechFlow Inc.") develops a new AI-driven logistics algorithm and incurs $900,000 in gross project spend across three items:

items: In-House Senior Developer Wages ($750,000 Gross): Five senior developers earning $150,000 each in Box 1 W-2 wages ($750,000 total) spend 80% of their working time coding and testing the experimental algorithm. A naive pro-rata calculation would multiply $150,000 × 5 × 80% = $600,000. However, under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2), because each developer spent at least 80% of their time performing qualified services ("substantially all"), 100% of their Box 1 W-2 wages qualify as QREs: $150,000 × 5 × 100% = $750,000, capturing an additional $150,000 of eligible wage QREs on Form 6765 Line 42 and Line 50.

Off-Premises AWS Development and Testing Servers ($50,000 Gross): TechFlow pays $50,000 to rent off-premises AWS cloud server capacity used exclusively to host the development and simulation testing environment (not commercial production hosting). While 100% of the $50,000 expenditure is eligible, it qualifies under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(4) as the rental or lease cost of off-premises computers (reported on Form 6765, Line 44 and Line 55), rather than tangible supplies under Section 41(b)(2)(C).

Third-Party Testing Contractor Invoice ($100,000 Gross): TechFlow pays an unrelated U.S. testing firm ("DesignLab") a $100,000 invoice to conduct systematic performance and reliability testing on behalf of TechFlow under a pre-existing written contract where TechFlow bears the economic risk of failure and retains rights to the results. Provided the testing evaluates technical and functional uncertainty rather than excluded cosmetic or style factors (IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B)), 65% of the invoice ($100,000 × 65% = $65,000) qualifies as Contract Research Expenses on Form 6765 Line 45 and Line 56.

body.text: Summing the three components, properly applying the 80% Substantially All wage rule increases TechFlow Inc.'s total validated QREs from $715,000 to $865,000 ($750,000 + $50,000 + $65,000), generating an additional $21,000 ($150,000 × 14%) in gross ASC research credit (or $16,590 in net reduced credit after the 79% Section 280C(c)(2) adjustment).
5. Strategic Compliance, Documentation, and Audit Defense

In the contemporary IRS enforcement environment—shaped by appellate and district court specificity precedents, IRS News Release IR-2021-203 (updated June 18, 2024, FAQ 21), the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG), and the comprehensive overhaul of IRS Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024; Instructions Rev. December 2025)—substantiating QREs can no longer be treated as a retrospective year-end estimation exercise.

Two federal court decisions catalyzed the IRS's shift toward mandatory upfront project-level disclosure. In Harper v. United States, 847 Fed. App'x 408 (9th Cir. 2021), the IRS challenged an R&D refund claim for failing to satisfy the specificity threshold of Treasury Regulation Section 301.6402-2(b)(1), which requires a claim to set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of its exact basis; although the Ninth Circuit ruled the IRS had waived its procedural objection by auditing the claim over four years, the litigation underscored the vulnerability of unsubstantiated filings. Shortly thereafter, in Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-890 (D. Utah July 15, 2022), the government challenged a Form 6765 refund filing that lacked project-level descriptions of the research performed, components developed, and specific allocations of wages and supplies to individual projects. Under IRS News Release IR-2021-203 (effective for refund claims filed after January 10, 2022) and updated as of June 18, 2024 (FAQ 21), taxpayers filing amended return refund claims must provide three mandatory elements at the time of filing: (1) identification of all business components to which the claim relates, (2) a clear description of all research activities performed for each business component, and (3) the total qualified employee wage, supply, computer rental, and contract research expenses for the claim year. While the June 18, 2024 update waived the initial filing requirement to list the names of the specific individuals who performed each research activity and the specific information each individual sought to discover, taxpayers must still maintain and produce those individual-level records upon examination.
5.1 Implementing Contemporaneous Documentation Protocols

Examiners routinely disallow QRE claims that rely on high-level cost-center estimates or uncorroborated year-end oral interviews. Taxpayers should execute two core operational protocols tailored to their industry profile.
Action Item 1 — Business-Component Technical Narratives

Taxpayers should establish a continuous engineering documentation workflow that records, for each specific business component (IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)), the three foundational inquiries embedded in redesigned Form 6765: (1) What did you make? (identifying the specific product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention and whether it is held for sale, lease, license, or internal use); (2) Why is it qualified? (documenting the specific technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design at the outset and the systematic process of experimentation—alternatives evaluated, simulations run, prototypes tested, and trial-and-error logs—conducted to resolve that uncertainty); and (3) How much did it cost? (project-level QRE breakdown). High-scrutiny industries must tailor these records to their specific audit risk areas: Manufacturing taxpayers must document experimental tooling, custom fabrication, and destroyed vs. commercial prototypes; Architecture and Engineering (A&E) firms must delineate qualifying structural/environmental experimentation from standard code-compliant design and review client contracts for funded-research exclusions; and Software Development enterprises must separate experimental algorithmic architecture from routine debugging, maintenance, or non-HTI internal-use software.
Action Item 2 — Contemporaneous Personnel Time-Tracking by Activity Tier

Because Section G of redesigned Form 6765 requires breaking down qualified wages for each business component into Direct Research (Line 50), Direct Supervision (Line 51), and Direct Support (Line 52), companies must configure payroll and project-management software with dedicated R&D project codes. Recording employee hours daily or weekly by specific business component and service tier substantiates when an engineer crosses the ≥80% Substantially All threshold (Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2)) and defends mixed-role executives (such as a Chief Technology Officer splitting time between first-line technical supervision and excluded corporate G&A) against IRS audit adjustments.
5.2 Navigating Post-OBBBA Financial Strategy (The IRC § 174A / § 41 / § 448 Interface)
With the enactment of P.L. 119-21 (OBBBA) and the issuance of Revenue Procedure 2025-28, tax directors must integrate QRE credit maximization with Section 174A deduction modeling.
Action Item 3 — Modeling 2022–2024 Unamortized R&E Recovery and the IRC § 448(d)(3) "Syndicate" Tax Shelter Trap

Consider a company that spent $1,000,000 per year on domestic R&E in 2022, 2023, and 2024 ($3,000,000 total). Under TCJA 5-year midpoint amortization, the company deducted $100,000 in 2022 (10%), $300,000 in 2023 (20% of 2022 plus 10% of 2023), and $500,000 in 2024 (20% of 2022 plus 20% of 2023 plus 10% of 2024), totaling $900,000 in cumulative deductions and leaving $2,100,000 of unamortized domestic R&E costs entering 2025. If the company spends another $1,000,000 per year in 2025 and 2026 and adopts immediate expensing under IRC Section 174A(a), electing 1-year full catch-up recovery under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) causes its 2025 R&E deduction to spike to $3,100,000 ($1,000,000 current 2025 expensing plus $2,100,000 unamortized catch-up), followed by $1,000,000 in 2026. Conversely, electing 2-year ratable recovery smooths total deductions to $2,050,000 per year in both 2025 and 2026 ($1,000,000 current expensing plus $1,050,000 unamortized recovery each year), while defaulting to the remaining 5-year TCJA schedule yields $1,600,000 per year in 2025 and 2026 ($1,000,000 current expensing plus $600,000 prior-year amortization).

When modeling this catch-up deduction, pass-through entities and small businesses must guard against the IRC Section 448 "syndicate" tax shelter trap. While IRC Section 448(c) establishes the small-business gross receipts test ($25 million base adjusted for inflation under Section 448(c)(4) to $31 million average annual gross receipts for 2025), IRC Section 448(a)(3) prohibits any "tax shelter" from using the cash method of accounting, and OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1)(A) disqualifies any tax shelter under Section 448(a)(3) from electing small-business retroactive Section 174A relief. Under IRC Section 448(d)(3)—which cross-references IRC Section 461(i)(3)(B) and IRC Section 1256(e)(3)(B)—the term "tax shelter" includes any "syndicate," defined as any partnership, S corporation, or non-C-corporation entity that allocates more than 35% of its losses for the taxable year to limited partners or limited entrepreneurs.

Consequently, if a pass-through entity accelerates $2,100,000 of unamortized 2022–2024 R&E deductions into 2025 (or deducts 2025 domestic R&E immediately) and tips from a net profit into a net tax loss for 2025 where more than 35% of that loss is allocated to passive limited partners or limited entrepreneurs, the entity automatically becomes a "tax shelter" under Section 448(d)(3) for 2025—forfeiting its eligibility for the cash method of accounting and small-business transition relief. To mitigate this hazard, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 provides a protective election allowing a taxpayer to rely on its 2024 income or loss allocations to determine whether it is classified as a syndicate for the 2025 taxable year. Small business taxpayers that were profitable in 2024 (or allocated 35% or less of 2024 losses to limited partners or entrepreneurs) should evaluate making this 2024 lookback election, or alternatively spreading unamortized recovery over two years (2025–2026), continuing the remaining 5-year schedule, or electing optional capitalization under IRC Section 174A(c) (≥60 months) or IRC Section 59(e) (10 years) to prevent triggering a syndicate net loss. Furthermore, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 Section 7.02(2)(f) clarifies that whether a taxpayer elects 1-year or 2-year recovery of its unamortized 2022–2024 domestic TCJA costs, that accelerated recovery continues to be characterized as "amortization," allowing it to be added back to Adjusted Taxable Income (ATI) when computing business interest deduction limitations under IRC Section 163(j).
Action Item 4 — Continuous General Ledger Segregation and Contract Review

Finance teams must maintain separate general ledger accounts for (1) non-depreciable tangible R&D supplies (Section 41(b)(2)(C), Form 6765 Line 43), (2) off-premises development and testing computer rentals and cloud server time-sharing (Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), Line 44), and (3) depreciable R&D capital equipment (Section 167, excluded from Section 41 QREs). Concurrently, legal and tax teams must review every third-party R&D contract prior to execution to verify that agreements where the company hires outside contractors explicitly place economic risk on the company and grant rights to the research results (Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3)), and agreements where the company performs research for clients make payment contingent on technical inspection/acceptance and preserve the company's substantial rights to reuse underlying technical data without paying royalties (Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d)).
5.3 Mastering Redesigned IRS Form 6765 Compliance (Sections A through G)

The IRS fundamentally redesigned Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) and its accompanying Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), expanding upfront disclosure from four sections to seven sections plus header elections.

At the top of Form 6765, Item A requires checking "Yes" or "No" to make the irrevocable IRC Section 280C(c)(2) reduced credit election on an original timely filed return (including extensions), while Item B requires disclosing whether the taxpayer is a member of a controlled group or business under common control under IRC Section 41(f)(1), which mandates attaching a group QRE and credit allocation statement. Section A (Regular Credit, Lines 1–13) and Section B (Alternative Simplified Credit, Lines 14–26) compute the gross credit and apply the Section 280C(c)(2) reduction (15.8% effective multiplier on Line 13 for the Regular Credit, or 79% multiplier on Line 26 for the ASC). Section C (Current Year Credit, Lines 27–32) reduces the research credit on Line 27 by any portion of the credit from Form 8932 (Line 2) attributable to differential wage payments that were also used to figure the research credit on Line 13 or Line 26; adds pass-through research credits from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts on Line 29; allocates estate or trust credits to beneficiaries on Line 31; and routes the net income tax credit on Line 32 to Form 3800 (General Business Credit), Part III, Line 4i (for eligible small businesses) or Line 1c (for all other filers). Section D (Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Election, Lines 33a–36) is completed by eligible QSBs checking Line 33a (and Line 33b if payroll taxes are reported under a different EIN via a PEO/agent) to elect up to $500,000 (Line 34) as a payroll tax offset transferred from Line 36 to Form 8974, Part 1, column (e).

Section E (Other Information, Lines 37–41) is mandatory for all filers reporting QREs on Line 48. It requires reporting: (Line 37) the total number of business components generating the QREs on Line 5 or Line 20; (Line 38) the dollar amount of officers' wages included on Line 42; (Line 39) whether the taxpayer acquired or disposed of any major portion of a trade or business during the tax year (triggering base-period adjustments under IRC Section 41(f)(3)); (Line 40) whether the taxpayer included any new categories or recharacterized categories of expenses as current-year QREs compared to base years (requiring corresponding base-year adjustments); and (Line 41) whether any QREs were determined following the Large Business and International (LB&I) ASC 730 Directive—which applies to taxpayers with assets of $10,000,000 or more that follow U.S. GAAP for Certified Audited Financial Statements (CAFS) showing R&D expenses separately and reconcile book-to-tax income on Schedule M-3—entering the amount from ASC 730 Directive Appendix C, Line 19 and attaching Form6765ASC730AppendixA.pdf, B.pdf, C.pdf, and D.pdf.

Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Question A and Lines 42–48) asks in Question A whether the filer is required to complete Section G (if required, Section G is completed first and its totals populate Section F; group members filing separate tax returns enter only their individual member QREs on Lines 42–47, while Line 48 reflects total QREs determined at the controlled-group level for credit computation). Section F segregates QREs across Line 42 (Total wages for qualified services, excluding Work Opportunity Credit wages), Line 43 (Total costs of supplies), Line 44 (Total rental or lease cost of computers), Line 45 (Total applicable amount of contract research, excluding basic research), Line 46 (Applicable basic research payments), Line 47 (Line 45 plus Line 46), and Line 48 (Total QREs = sum of Lines 42, 43, 44, and 47).

Section G (Business Component Information, Columns 49(a)–(f) and Lines 50–56) is optional for all filers for taxable years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return) and mandatory for taxable years beginning after 2025 unless the taxpayer qualifies for an exemption. A taxpayer is exempt from completing Section G if: (1) it is a Qualified Small Business under Section 41(h)(3) that checked the box in Section D to claim a reduced payroll tax credit, or (2) its total controlled-group QREs on Line 48 are $1.5 million or less, its controlled-group average annual gross receipts for the prior three taxable years (under Section 448(c)(3)) are $50 million or less, and it is claiming the research credit on an original return. Non-exempt filers must satisfy the 80% / Top 50 Business Component Rule, listing business components in descending order of total QREs until they have itemized at least 80% of total QREs reported on Line 48, up to a maximum of 50 business components, and reporting any remaining components on a single line labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) with aggregate dollar amounts in Columns 50–56. (If a taxpayer uses the ASC 730 Directive and its single "ASC 730 Directive" entry accounts for at least 80% of Line 48 QREs, no additional business components need be listed; if a taxpayer uses statistical sampling under Revenue Procedure 2011-42, it must still report the 80%/Top 50 components, append the word "sample" to sampled component identifiers in Column 49(c), and attach Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf).
